Consider the following differential equation y″−4y′+5y=xe2x.

The general solution to this equation can be written as y(x)=e2x(Acos⁡x+Bsin⁡x)+g(x), where A and B are constants. Which of the following could be the function g(x)?

Hint: Use the variation of parameters method. You may also wish to make use of the following results (integration constants omitted): ∫xsin⁡xdx=sin⁡x−xcos⁡x∫xcos⁡xdx=cos⁡x+xsin⁡x

a
2xe2x
b
2x2e2x
c
x2e2x
d
4xe2x
e
xe2x
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Suppose we have a second-order linear differential equation with linearly independent fundamental solutions y1(x) and y2(x). Then, according to the method of variation of parameters, we can seek a particular solution yp using the ansatz yp(x)=u1(x)y1(x)+u2(x)y2(x), where u1 and u2 satisfy the following system: {u1′y1′+u2′y2′=f(x)u1′y1+u2′y2=0

The solution to this system is u1(x)=−∫f(x)y2(x)W(y1,y2)dx,u2(x)=∫f(x)y1(x)W(y1,y2)dx, where W(y1,y2) is the Wronskian.

First, we note that the forcing term is f(x)=xe2x.

From the given information, we see that the complementary solution is yc(x)=e2x(Acos⁡x+Bsin⁡x).

Therefore, the fundamental solutions to the corresponding homogeneous equation are y1(x)=e2xcos⁡x,y2(x)=e2xsin⁡x.

We can use the method of variation of parameters if these solutions are linearly independent. So, let's first compute the Wronskian: W(y1,y2)=|y1y2y1′y2′|=y1(x)y2′(x)−y1′(x)y2(x)=(e2xcos⁡x)(e2xsin⁡x)′−(e2xcos⁡x)′(e2xsin⁡x)=(e2xcos⁡x)(2e2xsin⁡x+e2xcos⁡x)−(2e2xcos⁡x−e2xsin⁡x)(e2xsin⁡x)=e4x(cos2⁡x+sin2⁡x)=e4x≠0

Since the Wronskian is not equal to zero, this confirms that the functions y1(x) and y2(x) are independent.

Let’s compute u1(x) and u2(x): u1(x)=−∫f(x)y2(x)W(y1,y2)dx=−∫xe2x⋅e2xsin⁡xe4xdx=−∫xsin⁡xdx=−(sin⁡x−xcos⁡x)=xcos⁡x−sin⁡xu2(x)=∫f(x)y1(x)W(y1,y2)dx=∫xe2x⋅e2xcos⁡xe4xdx=∫xcos⁡xdx=cos⁡x+xsin⁡x

Therefore, the particular solution is yp(x)=u1y1+u2y2=(xcos⁡x−sin⁡x)(e2xcos⁡x)+(cos⁡x+xsin⁡x)(e2xsin⁡x)=e2x(xcos2⁡x−sin⁡xcos⁡x+sin⁡xcos⁡x+xsin2⁡x)=xe2x.

The general solution is the sum of the complementary and particular solutions, and can be written as follows: y(x)=yc(x)+yp(x)=e2x(Acos⁡x+Bsin⁡x)+xe2x⏟g(x)

Therefore, we conclude that g(x)=xe2x.

content.problem:
Consider the following differential equation

$$
{y}^{″}-4{y}^{′}+5y=x{e}^{2x}.
$$

The general solution to this equation can be written as

$$
y(x)={e}^{2x}\,(A\operatorname{cos}⁡x+B\operatorname{sin}⁡x)+g(x),
$$

where $A$ and $B$ are constants. Which of the following could be the function $g(x)?$

*Hint: Use the variation of parameters method. You may also wish to make use of the following results (integration constants omitted):*

$$
\begin{aligned}\int x\operatorname{sin}⁡x\,\text{d}x & =\operatorname{sin}⁡x-x\operatorname{cos}⁡x \\ \int x\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\text{d}x & =\operatorname{cos}⁡x+x\operatorname{sin}⁡x\end{aligned}
$$
content.worked_solution:
Suppose we have a second-order linear differential equation with linearly independent fundamental solutions ${y}_{1}(x)$ and ${y}_{2}(x).$ Then, according to the method of variation of parameters, we can seek a particular solution ${y}_{p}$ using the ansatz

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{p}(x) & ={u}_{1}(x){y}_{1}(x)+{u}_{2}(x){y}_{2}(x),\end{aligned}
$$

where ${u}_{1}$ and ${u}_{2}$ satisfy the following system:

$$
{\begin{aligned}{u}_{1}^{′}{y}_{1}^{′}+{u}_{2}^{′}{y}_{2}^{′}=f(x) \\ {u}_{1}^{′}{y}_{1}+{u}_{2}^{′}{y}_{2}=0\end{aligned}
$$

The solution to this system is

$$
{u}_{1}(x)=-\int \frac{f(x){y}_{2}(x)}{W({y}_{1},{y}_{2})}\,dx,\,{u}_{2}(x)=\int \frac{f(x){y}_{1}(x)}{W({y}_{1},{y}_{2})}\,dx,
$$

where $W({y}_{1},{y}_{2})$ is the Wronskian.

First, we note that the forcing term is $f(x)=x{e}^{2x}.$

From the given information, we see that the complementary solution is

$$
{y}_{c}(x)={e}^{2x}\,(A\operatorname{cos}⁡x+B\operatorname{sin}⁡x).
$$

Therefore, the fundamental solutions to the corresponding homogeneous equation are

$$
{y}_{1}(x)={e}^{2x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x,\,{y}_{2}(x)={e}^{2x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x.
$$

We can use the method of variation of parameters if these solutions are linearly independent. So, let's first compute the Wronskian:

$$
\begin{aligned}W({y}_{1},{y}_{2}) & =|\begin{aligned}{y}_{1} & {y}_{2} \\ {y}_{1}^{′} & {y}_{2}^{′}\end{aligned}| \\  & ={y}_{1}(x){y}_{2}^{′}(x)-{y}_{1}^{′}(x){y}_{2}(x) \\  & =({e}^{2x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x)({e}^{2x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x)^{′}-({e}^{2x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x)^{′}({e}^{2x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x) \\  & =({e}^{2x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x)(2{e}^{2x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x+{e}^{2x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x)-(2{e}^{2x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x-{e}^{2x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x)({e}^{2x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x) \\  & ={e}^{4x}({cos}^{2}⁡x+{sin}^{2}⁡x) \\  & ={e}^{4x}\ne 0\end{aligned}
$$

Since the Wronskian is not equal to zero, this confirms that the functions ${y}_{1}(x)$ and ${y}_{2}(x)$ are independent.

Let’s compute ${u}_{1}(x)$ and ${u}_{2}(x)$:

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}_{1}(x) & =-\int \frac{f(x){y}_{2}(x)}{W({y}_{1},{y}_{2})}\,dx \\  & =-\int \frac{x{e}^{2x}\cdot {e}^{2x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x}{{e}^{4x}}\,dx \\  & =-\int x\operatorname{sin}⁡x\,dx \\  & =-(\operatorname{sin}⁡x-x\operatorname{cos}⁡x) \\  & =x\operatorname{cos}⁡x-\operatorname{sin}⁡x \\ {u}_{2}(x) & =\int \frac{f(x){y}_{1}(x)}{W({y}_{1},{y}_{2})}\,dx \\  & =\int \frac{x{e}^{2x}\cdot {e}^{2x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x}{{e}^{4x}}\,dx \\  & =\int x\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,dx \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡x+x\operatorname{sin}⁡x\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the particular solution is

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{p}(x) & ={u}_{1}{y}_{1}+{u}_{2}{y}_{2} \\  & =(x\operatorname{cos}⁡x-\operatorname{sin}⁡x)({e}^{2x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x)+(\operatorname{cos}⁡x+x\operatorname{sin}⁡x)({e}^{2x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x) \\  & ={e}^{2x}\,(x{cos}^{2}⁡x-\operatorname{sin}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡x+\operatorname{sin}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡x+x{sin}^{2}⁡x) \\  & =x{e}^{2x}.\end{aligned}
$$

The general solution is the sum of the complementary and particular solutions, and can be written as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}y(x) & ={y}_{c}(x)+{y}_{p}(x) \\  & ={e}^{2x}\,(A\operatorname{cos}⁡x+B\operatorname{sin}⁡x)+{{x{e}^{2x}}_{⏟}}_{g(x)}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we conclude that

$$
g(x)=x{e}^{2x}.
$$

Question 9
?

Consider the following differential equation y″−2y′+5y=4excsc⁡2x.

The general solution to this equation can be written as y(x)=(Acos⁡2x+Bsin⁡2x)ex+g(x), where A and B are constants. Which of the following could be the function g(x)?

Hint: Use the variation of parameters method. You may also wish to make use of the following result (integration constant omitted): ∫cos⁡2xsin⁡2xdx=12ln⁡|sin⁡2x|

a
(sin⁡2xln⁡|sin⁡2x|+xcos⁡2x)ex
b
(sin⁡2xln⁡|sin⁡2x|−4xcos⁡2x)ex
c
(cos⁡2xln⁡|sin⁡2x|+2xsin⁡2x)ex
d
(cos⁡2xln⁡|sin⁡2x|−xsin⁡2x)ex
e
(sin⁡2xln⁡|sin⁡2x|−2xcos⁡2x)ex
Submit

decision.explanation: For y1=e^x cos(2x) and y2=e^x sin(2x), the Wronskian is 2e^{2x}. Variation of parameters gives u1=-∫2 dx=-2x and u2=∫2cot(2x) dx=ln|sin(2x)|. Therefore g=u1y1+u2y2=e^x(sin(2x)ln|sin(2x)|-2x cos(2x)), which is option e, on intervals where sin(2x)≠0.

after.name: Question 9
after.problem:
Consider the following differential equation

$$
{y}^{″}-2{y}^{′}+5y=4{e}^{x}\operatorname{csc}⁡2x.
$$

The general solution to this equation can be written as

$$
y(x)=(A\operatorname{cos}⁡2x+B\operatorname{sin}⁡2x){e}^{x}+g(x),
$$

where $A$ and $B$ are constants. Which of the following could be the function $g(x)?$

*Hint: Use the variation of parameters method. You may also wish to make use of the following result (integration constant omitted):*

$$
\int \frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡2x}{\operatorname{sin}⁡2x}\,dx=\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡|\operatorname{sin}⁡2x|
$$
after.worked_solution:
Suppose we have a second-order linear differential equation with linearly independent fundamental solutions ${y}_{1}(x)$ and ${y}_{2}(x).$ Then, according to the method of variation of parameters, we can seek a particular solution ${y}_{p}$ using the ansatz

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{p}(x) & ={u}_{1}(x){y}_{1}(x)+{u}_{2}(x){y}_{2}(x),\end{aligned}
$$

where ${u}_{1}$ and ${u}_{2}$ satisfy the following system:

$$
{\begin{aligned}{u}_{1}^{′}{y}_{1}^{′}+{u}_{2}^{′}{y}_{2}^{′}=f(x) \\ {u}_{1}^{′}{y}_{1}+{u}_{2}^{′}{y}_{2}=0\end{aligned}
$$

The solution to this system is

$$
{u}_{1}(x)=-\int \frac{f(x){y}_{2}(x)}{W({y}_{1},{y}_{2})}\,dx,\,{u}_{2}(x)=\int \frac{f(x){y}_{1}(x)}{W({y}_{1},{y}_{2})}\,dx,
$$

where $W({y}_{1},{y}_{2})$ is the Wronskian.

First, we note that the forcing term is $f(x)=4{e}^{x}\operatorname{csc}⁡2x.$

From the given information, we see that the complementary solution is

$$
{y}_{c}(x)=(A\operatorname{cos}⁡2x+B\operatorname{sin}⁡2x){e}^{x}.
$$

Therefore, the fundamental solutions to the corresponding homogeneous equation are

$$
{y}_{1}(x)={e}^{x}\operatorname{cos}⁡2x,\,{y}_{2}(x)={e}^{x}\operatorname{sin}⁡2x.
$$

We can use the method of variation of parameters if these solutions are linearly independent. So, let's first compute the Wronskian:

$$
\begin{aligned}W({y}_{1},{y}_{2}) & =|\begin{aligned}{y}_{1} & {y}_{2} \\ {y}_{1}^{′} & {y}_{2}^{′}\end{aligned}| \\  & ={y}_{1}(x){y}_{2}^{′}(x)-{y}_{1}^{′}(x){y}_{2}(x) \\  & =({e}^{x}\operatorname{cos}⁡2x)({e}^{x}\operatorname{sin}⁡2x)^{′}-({e}^{x}\operatorname{cos}⁡2x)^{′}({e}^{x}\operatorname{sin}⁡2x) \\  & =({e}^{x}\operatorname{cos}⁡2x)({e}^{x}\operatorname{sin}⁡2x+2{e}^{x}\operatorname{cos}⁡2x)-({e}^{x}\operatorname{cos}⁡2x-2{e}^{x}\operatorname{sin}⁡2x)({e}^{x}\operatorname{sin}⁡2x) \\  & ={e}^{2x}\operatorname{cos}⁡2x\operatorname{sin}⁡2x+2{e}^{2x}{cos}^{2}⁡2x-{e}^{2x}\operatorname{cos}⁡2x\operatorname{sin}⁡2x+2{e}^{2x}{sin}^{2}⁡2x \\  & =2{e}^{2x}({cos}^{2}⁡2x+{sin}^{2}⁡2x) \\  & =2{e}^{2x}\ne 0\end{aligned}
$$

Since the Wronskian is not equal to zero, this confirms that the functions ${y}_{1}(x)$ and ${y}_{2}(x)$ are independent.

Let’s compute ${u}_{1}(x)$ and ${u}_{2}(x)$:

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}_{1}(x) & =-\int \frac{f(x){y}_{2}(x)}{W({y}_{1},{y}_{2})}\,dx \\  & =-\int \frac{4{e}^{x}\operatorname{csc}⁡2x\cdot {e}^{x}\operatorname{sin}⁡2x}{2{e}^{2x}}\,dx \\  & =-2\int dx \\  & =-2x \\ {u}_{2}(x) & =\int \frac{f(x){y}_{1}(x)}{W({y}_{1},{y}_{2})}\,dx \\  & =\int \frac{4{e}^{x}\operatorname{csc}⁡2x\cdot {e}^{x}\operatorname{cos}⁡2x}{2{e}^{2x}}\,dx \\  & =2\int \frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡2x}{\operatorname{sin}⁡2x}\,dx \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡|\operatorname{sin}⁡2x|\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the particular solution is

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{p}(x) & ={u}_{1}{y}_{1}+{u}_{2}{y}_{2} \\  & =(-2x)({e}^{x}\operatorname{cos}⁡2x)+(\operatorname{ln}⁡|\operatorname{sin}⁡2x|)({e}^{x}\operatorname{sin}⁡2x) \\  & =(\operatorname{sin}⁡2x\operatorname{ln}⁡|\operatorname{sin}⁡2x|-2x\operatorname{cos}⁡2x){e}^{x}.\end{aligned}
$$

The general solution is the sum of the complementary and particular solutions, and can be written as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}y(x) & ={y}_{c}(x)+{y}_{p}(x) \\  & =(A\operatorname{cos}⁡2x+B\operatorname{sin}⁡2x){e}^{x}+{{(\operatorname{sin}⁡2x\operatorname{ln}⁡|\operatorname{sin}⁡2x|-2x\operatorname{cos}⁡2x){e}^{x}}_{⏟}}_{g(x)}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we conclude that

$$
g(x)=(\operatorname{sin}⁡2x\operatorname{ln}⁡|\operatorname{sin}⁡2x|-2x\operatorname{cos}⁡2x){e}^{x}.
$$

Since the Wronskian is not equal to zero, this confirms that the functions y1(x) and y2(x) are independent.

Let’s compute u1(x) and u2(x): u1(x)=−∫f(x)y2(x)W(y1,y2)dx=−∫4excsc⁡2x⋅exsin⁡2x2e2xdx=−2∫dx=−2xu2(x)=∫f(x)y1(x)W(y1,y2)dx=∫4excsc⁡2x⋅excos⁡2x2e2xdx=2∫cos⁡2xsin⁡2xdx=ln⁡|sin⁡2x|

content.problem:
Consider the following differential equation

$$
{y}^{″}-2{y}^{′}+5y=4{e}^{x}\operatorname{csc}⁡2x.
$$

The general solution to this equation can be written as

$$
y(x)=(A\operatorname{cos}⁡2x+B\operatorname{sin}⁡2x){e}^{x}+g(x),
$$

where $A$ and $B$ are constants. Which of the following could be the function $g(x)?$

*Hint: Use the variation of parameters method. You may also wish to make use of the following result (integration constant omitted):*

$$
\int \frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡2x}{\operatorname{sin}⁡2x}\,dx=\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡|\operatorname{sin}⁡2x|
$$
content.worked_solution:
Suppose we have a second-order linear differential equation with linearly independent fundamental solutions ${y}_{1}(x)$ and ${y}_{2}(x).$ Then, according to the method of variation of parameters, we can seek a particular solution ${y}_{p}$ using the ansatz

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{p}(x) & ={u}_{1}(x){y}_{1}(x)+{u}_{2}(x){y}_{2}(x),\end{aligned}
$$

where ${u}_{1}$ and ${u}_{2}$ satisfy the following system:

$$
{\begin{aligned}{u}_{1}^{′}{y}_{1}^{′}+{u}_{2}^{′}{y}_{2}^{′}=f(x) \\ {u}_{1}^{′}{y}_{1}+{u}_{2}^{′}{y}_{2}=0\end{aligned}
$$

The solution to this system is

$$
{u}_{1}(x)=-\int \frac{f(x){y}_{2}(x)}{W({y}_{1},{y}_{2})}\,dx,\,{u}_{2}(x)=\int \frac{f(x){y}_{1}(x)}{W({y}_{1},{y}_{2})}\,dx,
$$

where $W({y}_{1},{y}_{2})$ is the Wronskian.

First, we note that the forcing term is $f(x)=4{e}^{x}\operatorname{csc}⁡2x.$

From the given information, we see that the complementary solution is

$$
{y}_{c}(x)=(A\operatorname{cos}⁡2x+B\operatorname{sin}⁡2x){e}^{x}.
$$

Therefore, the fundamental solutions to the corresponding homogeneous equation are

$$
{y}_{1}(x)={e}^{x}\operatorname{cos}⁡2x,\,{y}_{2}(x)={e}^{x}\operatorname{sin}⁡2x.
$$

We can use the method of variation of parameters if these solutions are linearly independent. So, let's first compute the Wronskian:

$$
\begin{aligned}W({y}_{1},{y}_{2}) & =|\begin{aligned}{y}_{1} & {y}_{2} \\ {y}_{1}^{′} & {y}_{2}^{′}\end{aligned}| \\  & ={y}_{1}(x){y}_{2}^{′}(x)-{y}_{1}^{′}(x){y}_{2}(x) \\  & =({e}^{x}\operatorname{cos}⁡2x)({e}^{x}\operatorname{sin}⁡2x)^{′}-({e}^{x}\operatorname{cos}⁡2x)^{′}({e}^{x}\operatorname{sin}⁡2x) \\  & =({e}^{x}\operatorname{cos}⁡2x)({e}^{x}\operatorname{sin}⁡2x+2{e}^{x}\operatorname{cos}⁡2x)-({e}^{x}\operatorname{cos}⁡2x-2{e}^{x}\operatorname{sin}⁡2x)({e}^{x}\operatorname{sin}⁡2x) \\  & ={e}^{2x}\operatorname{cos}⁡2x\operatorname{sin}⁡2x+2{e}^{2x}{cos}^{2}⁡2x-{e}^{2x}\operatorname{cos}⁡2x\operatorname{sin}⁡2x+2{e}^{2x}{sin}^{2}⁡2x \\  & =2{e}^{2x}({cos}^{2}⁡2x+{sin}^{2}⁡2x) \\  & =2{e}^{2x}\ne 0\end{aligned}
$$

Since the Wronskian is not equal to zero, this confirms that the functions ${y}_{1}(x)$ and ${y}_{2}(x)$ are independent.

Let’s compute ${u}_{1}(x)$ and ${u}_{2}(x)$:

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}_{1}(x) & =-\int \frac{f(x){y}_{2}(x)}{W({y}_{1},{y}_{2})}\,dx \\  & =-\int \frac{4{e}^{x}\operatorname{csc}⁡2x\cdot {e}^{x}\operatorname{sin}⁡2x}{2{e}^{2x}}\,dx \\  & =-2\int dx \\  & =-2x \\ {u}_{2}(x) & =\int \frac{f(x){y}_{1}(x)}{W({y}_{1},{y}_{2})}\,dx \\  & =\int \frac{4{e}^{x}\operatorname{csc}⁡2x\cdot {e}^{x}\operatorname{cos}⁡2x}{2{e}^{2x}}\,dx \\  & =2\int \frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡2x}{\operatorname{sin}⁡2x}\,dx \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡|\operatorname{sin}⁡2x|\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the particular solution is

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{p}(x) & ={u}_{1}{y}_{1}+{u}_{2}{y}_{2} \\  & =(-2x)({e}^{x}\operatorname{cos}⁡2x)+(\operatorname{ln}⁡|\operatorname{sin}⁡2x|)({e}^{x}\operatorname{sin}⁡2x) \\  & =(\operatorname{sin}⁡2x\operatorname{ln}⁡|\operatorname{sin}⁡2x|-2x\operatorname{cos}⁡2x){e}^{x}.\end{aligned}
$$

The general solution is the sum of the complementary and particular solutions, and can be written as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}y(x) & ={y}_{c}(x)+{y}_{p}(x) \\  & =(A\operatorname{cos}⁡2x+B\operatorname{sin}⁡2x){e}^{x}+{{(\operatorname{sin}⁡2x\operatorname{ln}⁡|\operatorname{sin}⁡2x|-2x\operatorname{cos}⁡2x){e}^{x}}_{⏟}}_{g(x)}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we conclude that

$$
g(x)=(\operatorname{sin}⁡2x\operatorname{ln}⁡|\operatorname{sin}⁡2x|-2x\operatorname{cos}⁡2x){e}^{x}.
$$

Question 10
?

Consider the following differential equation y″+2y′+2y=e−xsec⁡x.

The general solution to this equation can be written as y(x)=e−x(Acos⁡x+Bsin⁡x)+g(x), where A and B are constants. Which of the following could be the function g(x)?

Hint: Use the variation of parameters method. You may also wish to make use of the following result (integration constant omitted): ∫tan⁡xdx=−ln⁡|cos⁡x|

a
e−x(cos⁡xln⁡|cos⁡x|−xsin⁡x)
b
e−x(sin⁡xln⁡|cos⁡x|+xcos⁡x)
c
xe−x(sin⁡xln⁡|cos⁡x|−xcos⁡x)
d
xe−x(cos⁡xln⁡|cos⁡x|+xsin⁡x)
e
e−x(cos⁡xln⁡|cos⁡x|+xsin⁡x)
Submit

decision.explanation: For y1=e^{-x}cos(x) and y2=e^{-x}sin(x), W=e^{-2x}. Variation of parameters gives u1=-∫tan(x)dx=ln|cos(x)| and u2=∫1 dx=x. Thus g=e^{-x}(cos(x)ln|cos(x)|+x sin(x)), option e, valid wherever cos(x)≠0.

after.name: Question 10
after.problem:
Consider the following differential equation

$$
{y}^{″}+2{y}^{′}+2y={e}^{-x}\operatorname{sec}⁡x.
$$

The general solution to this equation can be written as

$$
y(x)={e}^{-x}(A\operatorname{cos}⁡x+B\operatorname{sin}⁡x)+g(x),
$$

where $A$ and $B$ are constants. Which of the following could be the function $g(x)?$

*Hint: Use the variation of parameters method. You may also wish to make use of the following result (integration constant omitted):*

$$
\int \operatorname{tan}⁡x\,\text{d}x=-\operatorname{ln}⁡|\operatorname{cos}⁡x|
$$
after.worked_solution:
Suppose we have a second-order linear differential equation with linearly independent fundamental solutions ${y}_{1}(x)$ and ${y}_{2}(x).$ Then, according to the method of variation of parameters, we can seek a particular solution ${y}_{p}$ using the ansatz

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{p}(x) & ={u}_{1}(x){y}_{1}(x)+{u}_{2}(x){y}_{2}(x),\end{aligned}
$$

where ${u}_{1}$ and ${u}_{2}$ satisfy the following system:

$$
{\begin{aligned}{u}_{1}^{′}{y}_{1}^{′}+{u}_{2}^{′}{y}_{2}^{′}=f(x) \\ {u}_{1}^{′}{y}_{1}+{u}_{2}^{′}{y}_{2}=0\end{aligned}
$$

The solution to this system is

$$
{u}_{1}(x)=-\int \frac{f(x){y}_{2}(x)}{W({y}_{1},{y}_{2})}\,dx,\,{u}_{2}(x)=\int \frac{f(x){y}_{1}(x)}{W({y}_{1},{y}_{2})}\,dx,
$$

where $W({y}_{1},{y}_{2})$ is the Wronskian.

First, we note that the forcing term is $f(x)={e}^{-x}\operatorname{sec}⁡x.$

From the given information, we see that the complementary solution is

$$
{y}_{c}(x)={e}^{-x}(A\operatorname{cos}⁡x+B\operatorname{sin}⁡x).
$$

Therefore, the fundamental solutions to the corresponding homogeneous equation are

$$
{y}_{1}(x)={e}^{-x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x,\,{y}_{2}(x)={e}^{-x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x.
$$

We can use the method of variation of parameters if these solutions are linearly independent. So, let's first compute the Wronskian:

$$
\begin{aligned}W({y}_{1},{y}_{2}) & =|\begin{aligned}{y}_{1} & {y}_{2} \\ {y}_{1}^{′} & {y}_{2}^{′}\end{aligned}| \\  & ={y}_{1}(x){y}_{2}^{′}(x)-{y}_{1}^{′}(x){y}_{2}(x) \\  & =({e}^{-x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x)({e}^{-x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x)^{′}-({e}^{-x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x)^{′}({e}^{-x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x) \\  & =({e}^{-x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x)(-{e}^{-x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x+{e}^{-x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x)-(-{e}^{-x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x-{e}^{-x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x)({e}^{-x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x) \\  & ={e}^{-2x}({cos}^{2}⁡x+{sin}^{2}⁡x) \\  & ={e}^{-2x}\ne 0\end{aligned}
$$

Since the Wronskian is not equal to zero, this confirms that the functions ${y}_{1}(x)$ and ${y}_{2}(x)$ are independent.

Let’s compute ${u}_{1}(x)$ and ${u}_{2}(x)$:

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}_{1}(x) & =-\int \frac{f(x){y}_{2}(x)}{W({y}_{1},{y}_{2})}\,dx \\  & =-\int \frac{{e}^{-x}\operatorname{sec}⁡x\cdot {e}^{-x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x}{{e}^{-2x}}\,dx \\  & =-\int \operatorname{tan}⁡x\,dx \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡|\operatorname{cos}⁡x| \\ {u}_{2}(x) & =\int \frac{f(x){y}_{1}(x)}{W({y}_{1},{y}_{2})}\,dx \\  & =\int \frac{{e}^{-x}\operatorname{sec}⁡x\cdot {e}^{-x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x}{{e}^{-2x}}\,dx \\  & =\int dx \\  & =x\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the particular solution is

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{p}(x) & ={u}_{1}{y}_{1}+{u}_{2}{y}_{2} \\  & =(\operatorname{ln}⁡|\operatorname{cos}⁡x|)({e}^{-x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x)+(\operatorname{sin}⁡x)(x{e}^{-x}) \\  & ={e}^{-x}(\operatorname{cos}⁡x\operatorname{ln}⁡|\operatorname{cos}⁡x|+x\operatorname{sin}⁡x).\end{aligned}
$$

The general solution is the sum of the complementary and particular solutions, and can be written as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}y(x) & ={y}_{c}(x)+{y}_{p}(x) \\  & ={e}^{-x}(A\operatorname{cos}⁡x+B\operatorname{sin}⁡x)+{{{e}^{-x}(\operatorname{cos}⁡x\operatorname{ln}⁡|\operatorname{cos}⁡x|+x\operatorname{sin}⁡x)}_{⏟}}_{g(x)}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we conclude that

$$
g(x)={e}^{-x}(\operatorname{cos}⁡x\operatorname{ln}⁡|\operatorname{cos}⁡x|+x\operatorname{sin}⁡x).

Question 10
?

Consider the following differential equation y″+2y′+2y=e−xsec⁡x.

The general solution to this equation can be written as y(x)=e−x(Acos⁡x+Bsin⁡x)+g(x), where A and B are constants. Which of the following could be the function g(x)?

Hint: Use the variation of parameters method. You may also wish to make use of the following result (integration constant omitted): ∫tan⁡xdx=−ln⁡|cos⁡x|

a
e−x(cos⁡xln⁡|cos⁡x|−xsin⁡x)
b
e−x(sin⁡xln⁡|cos⁡x|+xcos⁡x)
c
xe−x(sin⁡xln⁡|cos⁡x|−xcos⁡x)
d
xe−x(cos⁡xln⁡|cos⁡x|+xsin⁡x)
e
e−x(cos⁡xln⁡|cos⁡x|+xsin⁡x)
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Suppose we have a second-order linear differential equation with linearly independent fundamental solutions y1(x) and y2(x). Then, according to the method of variation of parameters, we can seek a particular solution yp using the ansatz yp(x)=u1(x)y1(x)+u2(x)y2(x), where u1 and u2 satisfy the following system: {u1′y1′+u2′y2′=f(x)u1′y1+u2′y2=0

The solution to this system is u1(x)=−∫f(x)y2(x)W(y1,y2)dx,u2(x)=∫f(x)y1(x)W(y1,y2)dx, where W(y1,y2) is the Wronskian.

First, we note that the forcing term is f(x)=e−xsec⁡x.

From the given information, we see that the complementary solution is yc(x)=e−x(Acos⁡x+Bsin⁡x).

Therefore, the fundamental solutions to the corresponding homogeneous equation are y1(x)=e−xcos⁡x,y2(x)=e−xsin⁡x.

We can use the method of variation of parameters if these solutions are linearly independent. content.problem:
Consider the following differential equation

$$
{y}^{″}+2{y}^{′}+2y={e}^{-x}\operatorname{sec}⁡x.
$$

The general solution to this equation can be written as

$$
y(x)={e}^{-x}(A\operatorname{cos}⁡x+B\operatorname{sin}⁡x)+g(x),
$$

where $A$ and $B$ are constants. Which of the following could be the function $g(x)?$

*Hint: Use the variation of parameters method. You may also wish to make use of the following result (integration constant omitted):*

$$
\int \operatorname{tan}⁡x\,\text{d}x=-\operatorname{ln}⁡|\operatorname{cos}⁡x|
$$
content.worked_solution:
Suppose we have a second-order linear differential equation with linearly independent fundamental solutions ${y}_{1}(x)$ and ${y}_{2}(x).$ Then, according to the method of variation of parameters, we can seek a particular solution ${y}_{p}$ using the ansatz

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{p}(x) & ={u}_{1}(x){y}_{1}(x)+{u}_{2}(x){y}_{2}(x),\end{aligned}
$$

where ${u}_{1}$ and ${u}_{2}$ satisfy the following system:

$$
{\begin{aligned}{u}_{1}^{′}{y}_{1}^{′}+{u}_{2}^{′}{y}_{2}^{′}=f(x) \\ {u}_{1}^{′}{y}_{1}+{u}_{2}^{′}{y}_{2}=0\end{aligned}
$$

The solution to this system is

$$
{u}_{1}(x)=-\int \frac{f(x){y}_{2}(x)}{W({y}_{1},{y}_{2})}\,dx,\,{u}_{2}(x)=\int \frac{f(x){y}_{1}(x)}{W({y}_{1},{y}_{2})}\,dx,
$$

where $W({y}_{1},{y}_{2})$ is the Wronskian.

First, we note that the forcing term is $f(x)={e}^{-x}\operatorname{sec}⁡x.$

From the given information, we see that the complementary solution is

$$
{y}_{c}(x)={e}^{-x}(A\operatorname{cos}⁡x+B\operatorname{sin}⁡x).
$$

Therefore, the fundamental solutions to the corresponding homogeneous equation are

$$
{y}_{1}(x)={e}^{-x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x,\,{y}_{2}(x)={e}^{-x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x.
$$

We can use the method of variation of parameters if these solutions are linearly independent. So, let's first compute the Wronskian:

$$
\begin{aligned}W({y}_{1},{y}_{2}) & =|\begin{aligned}{y}_{1} & {y}_{2} \\ {y}_{1}^{′} & {y}_{2}^{′}\end{aligned}| \\  & ={y}_{1}(x){y}_{2}^{′}(x)-{y}_{1}^{′}(x){y}_{2}(x) \\  & =({e}^{-x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x)({e}^{-x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x)^{′}-({e}^{-x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x)^{′}({e}^{-x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x) \\  & =({e}^{-x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x)(-{e}^{-x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x+{e}^{-x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x)-(-{e}^{-x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x-{e}^{-x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x)({e}^{-x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x) \\  & ={e}^{-2x}({cos}^{2}⁡x+{sin}^{2}⁡x) \\  & ={e}^{-2x}\ne 0\end{aligned}
$$

Since the Wronskian is not equal to zero, this confirms that the functions ${y}_{1}(x)$ and ${y}_{2}(x)$ are independent.

Let’s compute ${u}_{1}(x)$ and ${u}_{2}(x)$:

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}_{1}(x) & =-\int \frac{f(x){y}_{2}(x)}{W({y}_{1},{y}_{2})}\,dx \\  & =-\int \frac{{e}^{-x}\operatorname{sec}⁡x\cdot {e}^{-x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x}{{e}^{-2x}}\,dx \\  & =-\int \operatorname{tan}⁡x\,dx \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡|\operatorname{cos}⁡x| \\ {u}_{2}(x) & =\int \frac{f(x){y}_{1}(x)}{W({y}_{1},{y}_{2})}\,dx \\  & =\int \frac{{e}^{-x}\operatorname{sec}⁡x\cdot {e}^{-x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x}{{e}^{-2x}}\,dx \\  & =\int dx \\  & =x\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the particular solution is

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{p}(x) & ={u}_{1}{y}_{1}+{u}_{2}{y}_{2} \\  & =(\operatorname{ln}⁡|\operatorname{cos}⁡x|)({e}^{-x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x)+(\operatorname{sin}⁡x)(x{e}^{-x}) \\  & ={e}^{-x}(\operatorname{cos}⁡x\operatorname{ln}⁡|\operatorname{cos}⁡x|+x\operatorname{sin}⁡x).\end{aligned}
$$

The general solution is the sum of the complementary and particular solutions, and can be written as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}y(x) & ={y}_{c}(x)+{y}_{p}(x) \\  & ={e}^{-x}(A\operatorname{cos}⁡x+B\operatorname{sin}⁡x)+{{{e}^{-x}(\operatorname{cos}⁡x\operatorname{ln}⁡|\operatorname{cos}⁡x|+x\operatorname{sin}⁡x)}_{⏟}}_{g(x)}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we conclude that

$$
g(x)={e}^{-x}(\operatorname{cos}⁡x\operatorname{ln}⁡|\operatorname{cos}⁡x|+x\operatorname{sin}⁡x).
$$
